judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: The element is the descriptor 'NHS Foundation Trust' (15px, bold) inside the header logo link, under the NHS lozenge and 'University Hospitals Birmingham'. The claim is true of the capture: white on #5795d0 from the pseudo-element is 3.17:1. Capture: the header is transparent and its ::before lays rgba(0,94,184,0.66) over a fixed full-page photo (.uhb-c-bg-image, page-background-home-2.jpg, a greyscale ward scene) that 'shows through the header'. In Rampa's full-page capture that photo sat at the bottom of the page, not behind the header, so the header read as flat #5795d0 (the screenshot shows #c6dbef, the same colour under the cookie notice's 66% white wash). A live render in Edge at 1280x800 shows the photo behind the header, and its pixels match a model of the photo under the blue overlay. So on the page users receive, the background behind the text is not a flat #5795d0. The cookie notice washes the whole page until it is dismissed; I judged the header after dismissal, since text behind a modal wash is not what is assessed. Live at scroll 0, the letters 'NH' sit on a light part of the photo at about 3.2:1, and the rest of the text is at 5.3:1 or more. This is normal-size text, so 4.5:1 applies, and the 'NH' falls short of it. But the text is the trust's organisational logo (NHS lozenge plus organisation name and descriptor, the link classed uhb-c-header__logo), and the 1.4.3 logotype exception ('text that is part of a logo or brand name') arguably exempts it. My lean is that the exception applies (no failure). Competent auditors would reasonably disagree: some treat live HTML header text as subject to 4.5:1. Hence uncertain.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is a news card image: a stock photo of network cables in a server, alt 'Microsoft outage'. It is not inside a link, and the card's h3 link 'Microsoft outage' follows it, with a summary. The claim is true of the capture: the alt is the story title, not a description of the cables. But the photo is a generic illustration that conveys nothing beyond the headline, and an alt naming the subject it illustrates serves its purpose here. 1.1.1 does not require describing a stock illustration's contents. At most the alt is redundant with the heading, and the better markup would be alt="" as decorative (an F38-style point). That is a different reason, and the claim, which asks for what the picture conveys, does not name it. The live page has the same card, image and alt. False positive.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is the footer SVG uhb-c-footer__vision: a swirl mark with the words 'Building healthier lives', visible in the footer. It has aria-hidden="true", focusable=false, and no title or desc. Neither the snapshot nor the live HTML has the text 'healthier lives' anywhere else, so the trust's slogan or vision statement, shown as an image of text, is not available to assistive technology. It conveys text, so it is not pure decoration. It needs a text alternative, and hiding it fails 1.1.1. The claim states exactly this. The live footer markup is identical. True positive.
